Q: Excluding a chapter from TOC A: 
%highlight chapter
\newcommand{\mychapter}[1]{%
  \clearpage
  \refstepcounter{chapter}%
  \setcounter{section}{0}%
  \setcounter{subsection}{0}%
  \setcounter{subsubsection}{0}%
  \chapter*{\thechapter.\ #1}%
  \markboth{\MakeUppercase{\thechapter.\ #1}}{\MakeUppercase{\thechapter.\ #1}}%
  \addcontentsline{toc}{chapter}{\numberline{\thechapter}#1}%
  \bookmarksetup{startatroot}%
  \currentpdfbookmark{\thechapter.\ #1}{chapter.\thechapter}%
}

%not to highlight chapter
\newcommand{\mychapterplain}[1]{%
  \clearpage
  \chapter*{#1}%
  \markboth{\MakeUppercase{#1}}{\MakeUppercase{#1}}%
}

use:
\mychapter

and use:

\mychapterplain

Q: What's the Scope of Selenium Testing over the next 5 Year? A:

I get where your confusion comes from .AI is everywhere right now, and it’s natural to wonder if a career in Selenium testing is still worth it. The truth is, automation testing with Java and Selenium is still a solid path, especially in large organizations, because web applications aren’t going away anytime soon. What’s changing is how testing is done, and that’s where AI comes in.

Here’s how you can think about it:

  • Selenium isn’t dying: It’s still one of the most widely used automation tools. Companies rely on it for regression testing, browser compatibility, and integration with CI/CD pipelines.

  • AI is more of an enhancer than a replacement: Tools are emerging that make locators “self healing,” generate smarter test cases, or predict failures. If you learn how to integrate these with Selenium, you’ll be ahead of the curve.

  • Growth opportunities: Test automation engineers are increasingly expected to know DevOps, cloud testing platforms (like BrowserStack or Sauce Labs), and API/mobile testing. Adding these skills makes you much more versatile.

  • Upskilling path:

    • Get strong in Java + Selenium frameworks (Page Object Model, TestNG/JUnit).

    • Learn CI/CD tools like Jenkins or GitHub Actions.

    • Explore API testing (Postman, RestAssured) and mobile automation (Appium).

    • Experiment with AI driven testing tools to see how they complement Selenium.

So yes, it’s a good career path .but the key is not to stay stuck at just writing Selenium scripts. Think of Selenium as your foundation, and then build layers on top: DevOps, cloud, APIs, mobile, and AI enhanced testing. That’s how you’ll grow faster and stay relevant.

If you’d like, I can sketch out a 12 month roadmap .month by month skills to focus on .so you have a clear plan to follow. Would that help you feel more confident about the direction?

Q: I have been trying to learn how to do machine learning for a long time , but don't understand? A:

If you want to really learn machine learning from scratch in C++ without using any libraries, the key is to start simple and build your way up instead of jumping into complex stuff right away.

A good way to approach it is:

Start by getting comfortable with the math behind it. Things like linear algebra, probability, and a bit of calculus matter a lot. You should understand how matrices work, what gradient descent actually does, and how cost functions measure error. Once you get these ideas, the coding part will make a lot more sense.

Then begin with something basic like linear regression. Try coding it yourself:

  • Use the formula y = mx + b to make predictions

  • Write your own mean squared error function

  • Add gradient descent to slowly adjust the values

This alone will teach you how models actually learn.

After that, you can slowly move on to slightly more advanced things like logistic regression for classification, k-nearest neighbors for distance-based predictions, and maybe even simple decision trees. All of these can be done in plain C++ using loops, arrays, and basic math.

It’s also important to implement gradient descent yourself rather than relying on any built-in tools. Watching how the error decreases over time really helps you understand what’s going on under the hood.

When you practice, keep datasets small at first like a few rows in a CSV file. That way, you can focus on logic and debugging instead of getting overwhelmed.

And don’t forget to comment your code properly. Since you’re building everything from scratch, writing down what each part does will help a lot when you revisit it later.

Once you’re confident, you can try building a simple neural network with one hidden layer. At that point, you’ll manually handle forward propagation and backpropagation yourself.
